claims.claim: Children and adolescents with ADHD show large working-memory deficits, worst for spatial storage and spatial central-executive tasks, so any multi-step maths done 'in the head' is where marks are most likely to be lost.
claims.source_title: A Meta-Analysis of Working Memory Impairments in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
claims.key_numbers: 26 studies (1997-2003). Effect sizes vs controls: spatial storage 0.85 (CI 0.62-1.08), spatial central executive 1.06 (CI 0.72-1.39), verbal storage 0.47 (CI 0.36-0.59), verbal central executive 0.43 (CI 0.24-0.62); deficits independent of language-learning disorder and IQ. Kasper, Alderson & Hudec 2012 (Clin Psychol Rev) later confirmed 'large between-group effect sizes' in both phonological and visuospatial domains (numbers not shown in search summary).
claims.implication: Multi-step maths (frequency trees, collecting terms, sign handling) is exactly where a spatial/central-executive deficit bites; the tutor skill's 'what's one thing you could write down?' rule is well aligned, but the fill-in widget that let her report arithmetic in prose removed the external record. Make written intermediate steps a hard requirement (a widget should not accept a final answer without at least one working line), keep every instruction short and visible on screen, and treat the recurring A4 sign and collecting-terms slips as a working-memory-load pattern to be re-tested under low load rather than as a knowledge gap.

claims.claim: Children and adolescents with ADHD judge elapsed time less accurately and less precisely than peers and tend to over-estimate durations, so her own sense of how long a task has taken or how much exam time is left cannot be relied on.
claims.source_title: Time Perception Deficits in Children and Adolescents with ADHD: A Meta-analysis
claims.key_numbers: Accuracy deficit Hedges' g > 0.40; precision deficit g = 0.66; higher tendency to overestimate time; not moderated by task type or stimulus modality, moderated by age and gender. A separate JAACAP meta-analysis of 55 studies found deficits largest for sub-second discrimination.
claims.implication: Do not rely on her sense of elapsed time: the parent and the skill should run a visible timer for every block, the tracker should store actual session length and duration_seconds on every practice run (neither is recorded today), and mock days (shape D) should train pacing explicitly against the clock, for example marks-per-minute checkpoints on Paper 3, because over-estimating time is the direction of error found.

claims.claim: Children and adolescents with ADHD show a medium-sized preference for small immediate rewards over larger delayed ones (delay aversion), which makes a GCSE nine months away a weak motivator and makes starting a session the hardest step.
claims.source_title: Choice-impulsivity in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A meta-analytic review
claims.key_numbers: 28 tasks from 26 studies, 4,320 children (2,360 ADHD, 1,960 typically developing); between-group g = 0.47; similar across delay-discounting and delay-of-gratification tasks. Marx, Hacker, Yu, Cortese & Sonuga-Barke 2021 (37 comparisons, 3,763 participants, 53% ADHD; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1087054718772138) found small-to-medium effects on both paradigms and that offering real rewards almost doubled the odds ratio.
claims.implication: The 'N days to the exam' badge and 'grade 5 in 2027' are distant rewards this profile discounts; motivation has to come from the next ten minutes. Keep the immediate score chart she likes, make every block end with an outcome shown at once (exit-ticket score, topic chip moving), open each session with a two-minute low-effort retrieval starter rather than a choice, and treat task initiation as the point of failure to instrument (log whether the session started on time). Real, tangible rewards agreed with the parent are more effective than symbolic ones; no study on procrastination itself in adolescents with ADHD appeared in the search results.

claims.claim: People with ADHD have a medium-sized deficit in stopping an already-prepared response, which is the mechanism behind answering before reading the whole question and answering every part when one was asked.
claims.source_title: Inhibitory control and psychopathology: a meta-analysis of studies using the stop signal task
claims.key_numbers: Stop-signal reaction time deficit in ADHD g = 0.62; study quality did not significantly affect the ADHD estimate.
claims.implication: Submitting answers without working, giving all three colours when only blues were asked, and 'skip it' are the response-inhibition signature, not carelessness. Add a forced pre-answer step to the maths tutor skill (restate in her own words what the question asks before the first line of working) and have both marker skills log 'read-the-question' and 'impulsive answer' as named error categories so the pattern appears on the dashboard instead of only in free-text watch notes.

claims.claim: On sustained-attention tests children with ADHD show a large overall deficit but only a small-to-moderate additional decline over time on task, so within-session fatigue is real but is not the main reason accuracy is lower.
claims.source_title: Evaluating vigilance deficits in ADHD: a meta-analysis of CPT performance
claims.key_numbers: 47 between-groups CPT studies; large effect sizes for overall performance; only small-to-moderate effect sizes for performance over time in the handful of studies reporting it; the authors attribute the smaller time-on-task effect partly to easy target/distractor discrimination in most tests. Exact g values not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: A within-session decline exists but is smaller than the overall attention gap, so shortening sessions alone will not fix accuracy; still, the 90-minute shape A has never been tested against her own data. Record how each session ended (finished, ran out, abandoned) and the position of each error within the session, then split or shorten blocks if late-session errors cluster; two full 90-minute sessions in one day (2 Sep) should not be the default.

claims.claim: ADHD performance depends on pacing: slow, sparse tasks produce disproportionate slowing and omissions, while very fast tasks produce more impulsive (commission) errors, so both a slow tutoring turn-taking rhythm and a speeding-up drill can each degrade her output in different ways.
claims.source_title: A meta-analytic study of event rate effects on Go/No-Go performance in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
claims.authors_year: Metin, Roeyers, Wiersema, van der Meere & Sonuga-Barke, 2012
claims.key_numbers: Significant, disproportionate reaction-time slowing in ADHD vs controls at slow event rates; larger effect sizes for commission errors at fast event rates; supports the state-regulation-deficit model. Exact effect sizes not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: Pace the work in both directions. Long reading passages and waiting for one hint at a time are slow-event-rate conditions that invite drift; the Spanish Shooting Gallery, which speeds up every three correct answers, is a fast-event-rate condition that invites commission errors, so its 71-81% accuracy should not be read as vocabulary knowledge. Keep the Gallery for fluency and engagement, log accuracy split by speed level (top_speed is already stored), keep tutoring turns short and frequent, and confirm knowledge with untimed retrieval before promoting a topic.

claims.claim: Strong, immediate reinforcement (a sizeable reward or a computer-game format) normalises task persistence in children with ADHD but does not normalise their working-memory performance, so engaging formats buy effort, not accuracy.
claims.source_title: Can Motivation Normalize Working Memory and Task Persistence in Children with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder? The Effects of Money and Computer-Gaming
claims.authors_year: Dovis, Van der Oord, Wiers & Prins, 2012
claims.key_numbers: Experimental case-control lab study: 30 children with ADHD vs 31 controls; four conditions (feedback-only, 1 euro, 10 euros, computer-game version). Feedback-only: ADHD worse on visuospatial working memory. Incentives improved ADHD working memory but even 10 euros and gaming did not normalise it; 10 euros and gaming normalised persistence of performance, 1 euro did not.
claims.implication: This is direct evidence that salient, immediate reinforcement, including a game format, restores persistence in ADHD without any streaks, badges or withholding, which supports keeping the score chart and the timed game as the parent has chosen. It also says game-like formats will not remove the working-memory cost, so written working and low-load re-tests remain necessary alongside them; weak token rewards (the '1 euro' analogue, a badge with no value to her) should not be expected to do anything.

claims.claim: NICE NG87 recommends individually assessed environmental modifications for every child or young person with ADHD, including shorter periods of focus with movement breaks, written reinforcement of verbal instructions and distraction control, and says medication should only be offered after such modifications have been implemented and reviewed.
claims.source_title: Recommendations | Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management | Guidance | NICE
claims.key_numbers: Listed modifications: seating, lighting and noise changes, reducing distractions (e.g. headphones), shorter periods of focus with movement breaks (including 'I need a break' cards), reinforcing verbal requests with written instructions, appropriate use of teaching assistants; to be specific to the person and determined from an assessment of needs. Also: ADHD-focused support for parents/carers (group-based, as few as 1-2 sessions), a holistic shared treatment plan covering educational needs, and consideration of CBT for young people still impaired after benefiting from medication (social skills, problem-solving, self-control). Update history shown: Jan 2023 (neurodevelopmental wording, ICD-11, group-based parent support), May 2025 (link to diagnostics guidance).
claims.implication: The NICE list maps directly onto session design: session shape A has no scheduled break (pausing only 'if frustrated'), so add a movement break every 20-25 minutes and an explicit word she can use to call one; put every task instruction in writing on screen rather than only in conversational prose; control distraction at the study desk; and record an individual needs assessment (what helps her) in the tracker instead of generic settings. Because NICE expects a shared treatment plan that covers educational needs and sequences medication after environmental modification, the parent should make sure whoever manages her ADHD knows she is sitting GCSEs at 13 and what adjustments are in place.

claims.claim: Organisational skills training produces moderate-to-large gains in organisation and inattention for children and adolescents with ADHD but only small gains in academic performance and grades, so it should be built in cheaply and judged by organisation first.
claims.source_title: Meta-analysis of organizational skills interventions for children and adolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
claims.key_numbers: 12 RCTs, 1,054 children (576 treatment, 478 control). Organisational skills: teacher-rated g = 0.54 (CI 0.17-0.91), parent-rated g = 0.83 (CI 0.32-1.34). Inattention: teacher g = 0.26 (CI 0.01-0.52), parent g = 0.56 (CI 0.38-0.74). Teacher-rated academic performance g = 0.33 (CI 0.14-0.51); GPA g = 0.29 (CI 0.07-0.51).
claims.implication: The best-evidenced non-drug intervention for this age group changes organisation more than marks, so implement its cheap components rather than a programme: a written start-of-session plan (what, how long, done-when), a materials checklist, and an end-of-session loose-ends list stored in the tracker, with the parent checking the plan was followed. Expect organisation and attention to improve before attempt grades do, and do not judge the change by grade alone.

claims.claim: In the SCCAP evidence-base update, organisation training is classed as a well-established treatment for adolescents with ADHD and behaviour-management approaches (parent training, contingency management) as well-established for children, whereas cognitive-training, neurofeedback and similar approaches do not reach that level.
claims.source_title: Evidence-Based Psychosocial Treatments for Children and Adolescents With Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
claims.key_numbers: Systematic review of literature 2012-2016 updating Evans, Owens & Bunford 2014 (J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol 43:527-551, which found behaviour-management interventions had the most robust support). 2018 update: organisation training well-established for adolescents; behavioural parent training well-established for children; combined training programmes Level 2 (probably efficacious) per search summary. A 2023 umbrella review (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37030086/) puts psychological interventions at SMD 0.42 for parent-rated and 0.25 for teacher-rated symptoms.
claims.implication: The system's strategy should follow this hierarchy: organisation and time-management training plus parent-delivered behavioural structure (clear expectations, monitoring, consistent agreed consequences) are the well-established options; working-memory or 'brain-training' apps, neurofeedback and diet changes are not. The parent's monitoring role is itself the evidence-based ingredient, so the dashboard should be designed to make weekly monitoring easy (plan followed, blanks, working shown) rather than only to display coverage.

claims.claim: The HOPS programme (organised materials, a planner with recorded tasks and dates, breaking work into segments, and checking with rewards) produced large parent-rated gains in organisation, planning and homework completion for 11-14-year-olds with ADHD, but no significant teacher-rated change.
claims.source_title: Evaluation of the Homework, Organization, and Planning Skills (HOPS) Intervention for Middle School Students with ADHD as Implemented by School Mental Health Providers
claims.key_numbers: 47 students (grades 6-8) randomised to HOPS or waitlist; 17 school mental-health providers in 5 districts; parent-rated organised action d = 0.88, planning d = 1.05, homework completion d = 0.85; no significant teacher-rated improvement. Langberg et al. 2018 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29172596/): 280 middle-school students randomised to HOPS, CHIEF or waitlist; both interventions improved parent-rated homework problems; effect sizes not shown in search summary. A cluster-randomised conceptual replication protocol (ages 11-14) was posted in 2026.
claims.implication: A brief home version is feasible: turn the tracker's 'planned next' field into a planner with due dates and a materials list, have the parent review it at the end of each session against what was done, and reward the routine itself rather than the marks. Because only parent ratings moved, verify progress with objective measures already in the tracker (attempts, exit tickets, blanks per paper), not with impressions of being more organised.

claims.claim: Response to the Challenging Horizons Program is heterogeneous (roughly a third to a half of adolescents make large gains and a quarter to two-thirds make little), and a strong adolescent-rated working alliance plus low parenting stress and parent-adolescent conflict predict who responds.
claims.source_title: Trajectories and Predictors of Response to the Challenging Horizons Program for Adolescents With ADHD
claims.key_numbers: Secondary analysis of the multi-site RCT (nine middle schools, three cohorts; N about 324-326; CHP after-school vs CHP mentoring vs community care). Depending on outcome, 16-46% made large improvements into the normal range and 26-65% made small or negligible improvements. Earlier RCT (Evans et al. 2011, 49 students, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21658528/) showed improvement in symptoms and impairment vs community care. A CrimeSolutions summary of the 2016 main trial states academic functioning and parent/teacher ADHD ratings did not differ significantly from control; primary effect sizes not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: Even a well-run adolescent programme leaves many non-responders, and relationship quality predicts response, so parent-run sessions should protect the relationship over enforcing compliance (the skill's warm brief tone and pause-when-frustrated rule are right). The tracker should flag non-response explicitly: if the behavioural metrics (blanks per paper, working shown) have not moved by the Dec 2026 checkpoint, change the approach rather than intensify it.

claims.claim: STAND, a parent-teen behaviour therapy with motivational interviewing that targets organisation, time management and planning plus parent monitoring, showed medium-to-large effects in its efficacy RCT but no intent-to-treat benefit over usual care when delivered by community therapists, with gains only when therapists were licensed.
claims.source_title: Parent-teen behavior therapy + motivational interviewing for adolescents with ADHD
claims.key_numbers: 2016 efficacy RCT: N = 128 ethnically diverse teens (78.5% Hispanic); medium-to-large improvements in ADHD symptom severity and impairment vs control; medium effects on symptoms and OTP skills when parents had elevated ADHD symptoms, depression or conflict. 2021 community effectiveness trial (https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(20)31375-7/abstract): 278 adolescents, 82 community therapists, 4 clinics, seven primary outcomes at about 5 and 10 months; no significant group x time effects in ITT. 3-year follow-up (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39442667/): no ITT differences; when therapists were licensed (22%), STAND gave superior hyperactivity/impulsivity, organisational skills and parent-teen conflict outcomes.
claims.implication: The transferable ingredient is the motivational-interviewing stance: the student sets the goal and chooses the order of work, the parent monitors and applies agreed consequences, and autonomy is supported rather than scripted. But the null community result means the parent should not expect a do-it-yourself version to reproduce trial effects; use it as a style for the weekly check (shape C) and the parent's oversight, not as a claimed treatment.

claims.claim: Self-regulation interventions, in which the student monitors and records her own attention or work quality at set intervals, are among the most effective classroom strategies for on-task behaviour, academic accuracy and productivity in children with ADHD symptoms.
claims.source_title: The Effects of Classroom Interventions on Off-Task and Disruptive Classroom Behavior in Children with Symptoms of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analytic Review
claims.key_numbers: Largest effects for consequence-based and self-regulation interventions; single-subject designs mean SMD = 3.61 (a single-subject metric not comparable to group g); positive effects on on-task behaviour, inappropriate behaviour, academic accuracy and productivity. A separate 10-study review found self-monitoring improved attention, assignment accuracy and completion.
claims.implication: Self-monitoring is cheap and fits a text tutor: add a self-check prompt to the maths skill every few questions ('Did I write working? Did I answer what was asked?') and a one-line self-rating at session end (focus, working shown) stored by tracker_log_session so the parent can see the trend. Treat the effect as promising rather than precise, because the numbers come from single-subject designs and are inflated.

caveats: The session-wide WebSearch budget was exhausted after 29 searches; four planned searches were refused: Dekkers et al. 2017 on time-on-task effects in ADHD (surfaced at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5701950/ but not read), the Sibley et al. 2025 JCPP Research Review on adolescent ADHD treatments (https://acamh.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jcpp.14056?af=R, content not shown), the maths error-types study in adolescents with ADHD (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5641671/), and a procrastination-ADHD association study.

Task initiation and procrastination: no meta-analysis, RCT or clinical study specific to adolescents with ADHD appeared in results; the search returned practitioner blogs and one 2005 study on executive and motivational processes in adolescents with ADHD (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1183187/). The delay-aversion literature (C3) is the nearest mechanism-level evidence and the claim about 'starting is the hardest step' is an inference from it.

Time-on-task decline (C5): Huang-Pollock et al. reported only a 'handful' of studies with performance-over-time data and no exact g was shown in the search summary. No study of optimal study-session length for adolescents with ADHD was found; NICE says 'shorter periods of focus' without a number, so the 20-25 minute figure in C8's implication is a design suggestion, not a guideline value.

Maths error link used in C1's implication: 'Working Memory and Math Skills in Children With and Without ADHD' (https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/features/neu-neu0000920.pdf) and 'Neurocognitive and Behavioral Predictors of Math Performance in Children with and without ADHD' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3966972/) report that working-memory deficits partially account for ADHD-related maths achievement deficits and describe procedural, carrying/borrowing and multistep errors and rapid responding; one study found no ADHD difference in maths accuracy; numbers not shown in search summaries.

All intervention trials found (HOPS, CHP, STAND, OST meta-analysis) are US school- or clinic-based with trained providers, children aged roughly 8-17, and no home-educated participants and no AI tutoring; transfer to a parent plus Claude-skill setting is inference. STAND's null community result shows delivery quality matters.

CHP: the CrimeSolutions programme summary states the 2016 main trial found no statistically significant differences in academic functioning or parent/teacher ADHD ratings vs control, while the trajectories paper shows heterogeneous response; treat CHP as evidence about who responds, not as evidence of reliable academic gain. Primary effect sizes were not shown in any search summary.

Evans et al. 2018 detail that 'combined training' is Level 2 (probably efficacious) came from a search summary that may have blended sources; the well-established status of organisation training for adolescents was consistent across summaries. A search summary attributed to Sibley et al. 2023 (Lancet Child & Adolescent Health) the statement that OST is well-established for adolescents and mindfulness-based interventions are newly supported; not verified.
Gaastra et al. 2016 (C14): the SMD of 3.61 is from single-subject designs and is not comparable to group-design effect sizes; the underlying self-monitoring studies are small.

NICE NG87 update history: the brief says '2018, updated 2019'; search results show further updates in January 2023 (ADHD described as a neurodevelopmental disorder, ICD-11, parent support to be group-based and ADHD-focused) and May 2025 (link to diagnostics guidance). NG87 does not cover exam access arrangements (extra time, rest breaks, prompter), which are a JCQ process outside this area key.

All executive-function meta-analyses (C1-C6) sample children and adolescents with diagnosed ADHD and give group-average effects; nothing in the system records this student's individual profile, diagnosis detail, medication status or comorbidities, so which of these deficits apply to her, and how strongly, is unknown. Several trials include medicated participants; effects of non-pharmacological measures may differ by medication status.

Dovis et al. 2012 (C7) is a single lab experiment with 30 ADHD participants using monetary and game incentives; it supports the direction (reinforcement restores persistence) but not any particular size of effect for a score chart or timed game.
